sections.title: When AI scores answers
paragraphs: Scoring every answer by hand does not scale. If you test five {{model}}s on 100 prompts, that is 500 answers to grade. A human can do ten carefully; automation can do hundreds in minutes.
Regression evals help you know when automation is worth trusting on a golden set — rerun the same prompts after each change before you scale batch judging.

A {{judge}} is a {{model}} you use to score other {{model}}s' answers. You send it the prompt, the answer, and the {{rubric}}, and it returns scores per {{criterion}} plus reasoning. If the {{judge}} was given clear anchors, its scores often align with human grading.

AiEval's "Run full automation" button does exactly this: generates answers from contestant {{model}}s, then calls a {{judge}} {{model}} to score them using your {{rubric}}. You review the scores instead of writing them from scratch.

This is not magic. The {{judge}} can miss nuance, favor certain styles, or apply {{criterion}} anchors inconsistently. That is why you spot-check: open Compare, read the answers, and see if the scores make sense.
Next: when to trust automation, and when to double-check by hand.
bullets: Automation scales evaluation from 10 to 1000 prompts.
Spot-check: automation is fast, not infallible.

check.prompt: Your team wants to evaluate 500 {{model}} answers. A colleague says: "Let's automate scoring with a {{judge}} and never read the answers." What is the risk?
check.answer: The judge may score inconsistently or miss errors humans would catch
choices: The judge may score inconsistently or miss errors humans would catch
Automation is slower than reading all 500 by hand
The judge will refuse to score and crash the system
check.explanation: {{judge}} {{model}}s scale evaluation but can misapply rubrics, favor certain wording, or miss subtle errors. Always spot-check a sample to ensure scores are trustworthy.

sections.title: What judges get right — and wrong
paragraphs: {{judge}} {{model}}s excel at surface-level checks: is the answer on-topic, does it include required elements, is the tone polite? They struggle with deep reasoning: is the medical diagnosis correct given symptoms, does the code logic handle all edge cases?
Click each scenario below to see where automation helps and where human review is critical. Notice that the {{rubric}} matters: vague criteria confuse judges as much as they confuse human reviewers.

When designing evaluations, consider which {{criterion}} rows are safe to automate (format, tone, completeness) and which need expert review (factual accuracy in a specialized domain, legal compliance).

Good practice: run automation first to filter obvious failures, then human-review the top-scoring answers to ensure quality. That hybrid workflow is faster than all-manual and more reliable than all-automated.

reveals.prompt: Criterion: Answer is polite and under 100 words. Can a judge score this reliably?
reveals.reveal: Yes — tone detection and word count are tasks {{judge}} {{model}}s handle well.

reveals.prompt: Criterion: Answer correctly cites the current tax law. Can a judge score this reliably?
reveals.reveal: Risky — the {{judge}} may not know current law or may hallucinate. Human expert review is safer.

reveals.prompt: Criterion: Code compiles and has no syntax errors. Can a judge score this reliably?
reveals.reveal: Better to run the code through a compiler than trust a {{judge}} to simulate syntax checking.

reveals.prompt: Criterion: Answer includes three actionable steps. Can a judge score this reliably?
reveals.reveal: Yes — counting structural elements is a task {{judge}}s handle consistently.

check.prompt: You built a {{rubric}} for medical advice answers. One {{criterion}} is "factually correct per latest guidelines." Should you trust a {{judge}} to score this alone?
check.answer: No — have a medical expert review high-stakes accuracy claims
choices: Yes — judges are always accurate on specialized facts.
No — have a medical expert review high-stakes accuracy claims
Yes — as long as the judge is a big model, it will know medicine.
No — never use automation for any scoring.
check.explanation: {{judge}} {{model}}s can hallucinate or apply outdated knowledge. For high-stakes domains (medical, legal, financial), expert human review is essential.

sections.title: Spot-check and refine
paragraphs: After running automation in AiEval, open the Compare page. Read a few answers, check if the {{criterion}} scores align with what you would give. If the {{judge}} scored politeness as 5 but the answer feels curt, that is a signal to adjust the {{rubric}} anchors or the {{judge}}'s prompt.

Common fixes: sharpen vague {{criterion}} wording ("helpful" → "answers the question with context"), add negative examples to anchors ("Score 1: ignores the question entirely"), or switch to a different {{judge}} {{model}} that handles your domain better.
Evaluation is iterative. Your first {{rubric}} will not be perfect, and the first {{judge}} run may surprise you. Refine based on what you see in Compare, re-run automation, and check again.
When automation aligns with your judgment on a sample, you can trust it to scale. When it does not, treat automation as a draft and apply human review.
bullets: Spot-check: read a sample of scored answers.
Iterate: run automation, review, improve, repeat.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what is a {{judge}} in LLM evaluation?
check.answer: A model that scores other models' answers
accept: a model used to evaluate answers
check.explanation: A {{judge}} is a {{model}} that reads prompts, answers, and rubrics, then assigns scores — automating the review step.
